p: Brighton Museum is an easy one to fit into a busy day. An hour or two is plenty for most people, and because it's all indoors it's a cracking option when the rain comes in sideways off the Channel. Have a look at the latest admission arrangements and what's on before you go, as exhibitions change through the year.

The collections are wide-ranging, and part of the fun is the variety. Decorative arts, fashion, paintings and objects from around the world sit alongside stories of Brighton's own people, so it's well suited to mixed groups where everyone wants something different.

Coming by train? Brighton station is roughly a fifteen-minute walk downhill, and the route through North Laine is a treat in itself, with quirky independent shops, vintage stores and cafés. Once you're at the museum, the Royal Pavilion is right next door, and Brighton Dome, the city's big concert venue, shares the same estate. So you can easily make a proper culture morning of it before the seafront calls.

From the museum it's a short stroll to the Lanes, the twisting alleys full of jewellers and little shops, and then down to the seafront. Brighton Palace Pier is the big draw for fun, with rides, arcades and doughnuts. If natural history is more your thing, the Booth Museum, a separate site up in the Dyke Road area, is another of the city's quirky collections. Whatever you pick, you'll be back by the sea in no time.
